query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In situ adaptive thermal control via dynamic interlayer heating/cooling modulation coupled with laser power adjustment during laser powder bed fusion of high-entropy alloys reduces rapid cooling-induced thermal gradients and residual stress, thereby minimizing fabrication-induced defects and improving dimensional precision and mechanical integrity relative to the standard process.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy components produced by standard L-PBF exhibit rapid cooling-induced residual stresses, dimensional distortions, porosity, and microcracks.
generation.intervention: In situ adaptive thermal control via dynamic interlayer heating/cooling modulation coupled with real-time laser power adjustment.
generation.conditions: Applied during the L-PBF process under typical high-energy deposition conditions for HEAs (e.g., rapid melting and solidification), where the standard process leads to significant thermal gradients.
generation.structural_mediator: A moderated thermal gradient and controlled cooling rate across layers that promote a more uniform grain structure and reduced residual stress.
generation.mechanism: Dynamic adjustment of interlayer temperature and laser power modulates the cooling rate by reducing peak thermal gradients during solidification. This controlled thermal profile diminishes residual stresses and limits defect formation such as porosity and microcracking, thereby ensuring better dimensional fidelity and enhanced mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the conventional process, the intervention will yield parts with lower residual stress levels, reduced defect density, tighter dimensional tolerances, and improved mechanical properties (e.g., higher tensile strength and ductility).
generation.baseline: Standard L-PBF processing of HEAs, which typically exhibits rapid cooling, large thermal gradients, high residual stress, and a high incidence of defects leading to dimensional inaccuracies and reduced mechanical integrity.
generation.boundary: The expected improvements should be achievable for common HEA compositions under typical L-PBF conditions. However, the effectiveness might diminish for alloys exhibiting extreme thermal conductivities or if the thermal modulation parameters are not optimally tuned, possibly affecting phase formation.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal modulation parameters (temperature set points and laser power adjustments) need further refinement, and the universality of the approach across different HEA formulations remains to be conclusively demonstrated.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of high-entropy alloy components using L-PBF: one set with the standard process parameters (control) and one with the proposed in situ adaptive thermal control intervention. Keep all other parameters (e.g., powder composition, layer thickness, environmental controls) identical. Use integrated sensors to monitor interlayer temperatures in real time and adjust laser power dynamically in the experimental group.
measurements: Defect density and size (using micro-CT scanning and SEM)
Dimensional accuracy (using a coordinate measuring machine)
Mechanical properties (tensile strength, ductility from mechanical testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the experimental group using in situ adaptive thermal control does not exhibit statistically significant improvements over the control group in at least two of the following metrics: reduced residual stress, lower defect density, improved dimensional precision, and enhanced mechanical performance.

The complex temperature cycle in L-PBF with a rapid cooling rate can cause thermal residual stress in the solidification substructure, which induces cracks. To further investigate the characteristics of the printed sample, the microstructure was characterized by SEM and EDX analyses, as shown in Figure 5a,b. Intergranular and transgranular cracks were observed in the printed sample. EDX analysis showed furthermore that the cracks were irregular, and their size was in the range from tens to hundreds of micrometers (Figure 5a,b). Quantitative analysis of the SEM images revealed that the average crack density decreased from 12.3 cracks/mm2 at a VED of 251.2 J/mm3 to 4.3 cracks/mm2 at a VED of 187.7 J/mm3, while the maximum observed crack length also decreased from 193.3 μm to 84.2 μm over the same range. This trend demonstrates a clear inverse relationship between VED and both crack density and crack length, consistent with findings in the literature that higher energy input can increase thermal gradients and residual stresses, thereby promoting crack formation, while lower VEDs may reduce cracking but risk lack of fusion or porosity. Many scholars have studied HEAs [,,], but most focus on design principles, metallurgical mechanisms, phase changes, micro-structures, and properties of HEAs manufactured by conventional technologies. Several AM methods have been successfully implemented to fabricate structures with HEAs []. The powder bed fusion (PBF) processes, specifically the selected laser melting (SLM) technique, have been widely adopted []. SLM is a powder-bed additive manufacturing technology, which is also advantageous for producing complex-shaped parts []. During the SLM process, rapid melting and solidification are attributable to short-time interaction between laser energy and metal powder, which facilitates the formation of fine microstructure and improves the mechanical properties of the parts []. Meanwhile, ultra-fast cooling helps prevent the formation of intermetallic compounds and element dissolution. Thus, SLM was recently also used for HEA manufacturing, and some studies on the manufacturing, microstructure, and tensile properties of these alloys have been reported []. decision.trend: Early studies largely addressed the challenges of additive manufacturing of high-entropy alloys by modifying the alloy system through dispersion strengthening (e.g., oxide coatings) and optimizing laser process parameters. Later efforts shifted to post‐processing thermal interventions—such as deep cryogenic treatment—to relieve residual stresses and improve mechanical properties. Most recently, deposition strategy modifications have been applied to mitigate crack formation and internal stress. Overall, the trend has moved from ex situ compositional and process tweaks toward integrating thermal management to indirectly control solidification defects, although a fully in situ solution that simultaneously ensures dimensional precision and mechanical integrity is still lacking.
decision.unsolved: The unsolved challenge is to implement a single, in situ intervention that curbs the rapid cooling-induced residual stresses and associated microstructural defects during the additive build while maintaining dimensional accuracy and mechanical robustness in high-entropy alloy components.
decision.lever: in situ adaptive thermal control via dynamic interlayer heating/cooling modulation coupled with laser power adjustment
decision.why: Building on the success of post‐processing treatments and recent in situ deposition strategy optimizations, an adaptive thermal management approach directly integrated during the laser powder bed fusion process is the logical next step. By dynamically controlling the thermal gradient and cooling rates, this intervention could reduce residual stresses and minimize defect formation while preserving the near-net shape precision required for high-entropy alloy components.
